title: A survey on large language model based autonomous agents
extended_summary:
This paper is a broad survey of large language model (LLM)-based autonomous agents. It asks how recent work has designed, equipped, and evaluated autonomous agents built on top of LLMs, rather than studying any educational intervention or learner outcome. The review organizes the field around three pillars: agent construction, application domains, and evaluation strategies.

The paper proposes a unified framework for agent architecture with four modules: profiling, memory, planning, and action. It then reviews how different works build agent capabilities through prompt-based strategies, external tools, memory systems, and fine-tuning on task-specific data. The survey also summarizes applications in social science, natural science, and engineering, along with common evaluation approaches.

The paper does not report a participant-based study, an intervention, or any K-12 literacy outcomes. No population of human learners is studied, and there are no subgroup analyses or accessibility-specific findings. Its main contribution is conceptual: taxonomy building, synthesis of prior work, and discussion of challenges and future directions in LLM-based autonomous agents.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a broad review article on LLM-based autonomous agents, not an empirical study of a K-12 AI tool or literacy intervention. It contains no participant-level educational outcomes, comparison groups, or subgroup analyses relevant to literacy.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is measured in the paper, so there is no outcome-based effect to assess. Any subgroup or accessibility claims are absent from the empirical record because no such study is reported.
